a: The man who raised me sold me
t: A slave raised in a household
p: Hermas opens his book as a former slave, sold by the man who brought him up.
b: The Greek ho threpsas me is 'the one who reared me'. Lake's footnote says the line is 'hardly intelligible' as it stands: 'presumably the meaning is that Hermas was born a slave, and that his owner sold him to Rhoda'; 'it is implied that he then passed out of her possession, and later on made her acquaintance again'; or the verb may mean only that he 'came to know her properly'. Either way the author of this long book about God's household began life as someone else's property. Elsewhere he has a wife, children and a business (6:2-3; 7:1), so he had become free.
orig: ὁ θρέψας με (ho threpsas me), 'the one who reared me'

a: in Rome
p: The Shepherd is set in and around the city of Rome, by the Tiber and on the roads into the country.
b: Rome is named in the first sentence, and the places that follow are Roman: the Tiber (1:2), the road toward Cumae on the Bay of Naples (1:3; 5:1), the Campanian Way (22:2). The old woman orders the book read 'in this city with the elders who lead the church' (8:3). Lake fixes the date and place from the Muratorian list, which says Hermas wrote 'in the city of Rome' while his brother Pius led the church there, about 148 in Lake's dating; he adds that 'many critics' think the book was written in stages over the twenty or thirty years before. Paul's letter to Rome greets a Hermas (Romans 16:14); whether he is this author is taken up on the book's opening pages.

a: bathing in the Tiber River
p: Hermas helps his former owner out of Rome's river, and one thought about her starts the whole book.
b: The Tiber runs through Rome to the sea at Ostia. Bathing in the river was ordinary; what matters is Hermas's courtesy and then his thought: 'I would be a happy man if I had a wife like her.' He insists it was only that, 'and nothing else at all'. The story is built so that the reader agrees with him, and then hears in 1:8 that even this was a sin. Lake's marginal heading here is 'Hermas and Rhoda'.

a: A spirit took hold of me and carried me off
p: Hermas is carried away as Ezekiel and John were, though the Greek here has no article: 'a spirit'.
b: Prophets in the Bible are lifted and carried by the spirit: 'A spirit lifted me up' (Ezekiel 3:12); 'He carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness' (Revelation 17:3). Hermas uses the same kind of language for his journey through a roadless, broken country. The Greek is pneuma without the article, so the Plain English Translation says 'a spirit', as Lake does ('a spirit seized me'); 5:1 has the same words. Whether Hermas means the Holy Spirit, an angel or his own spirit in a trance, he does not say.
r: Ezekiel 3:12; Ezekiel 3:14; Ezekiel 8:3; Revelation 17:3; Revelation 21:10; 2 Corinthians 12:2-4

a: the sky opened
p: The opening of heaven is the standard start of a vision in Jewish and Christian writing.
b: 'The heavens were opened' begins Ezekiel's visions (Ezekiel 1:1), and the same picture stands at Jesus' baptism, at Stephen's death and at the start of John's visions (Mark 1:10; Acts 7:56; Revelation 4:1). Hermas's opening is unusual only for who looks down at him: not an angel or the Lord, but the woman he had looked at in the river. The Greek ouranos is both 'sky' and 'heaven'; it is shut again in 2:1.

a: Lady
t: Lady, sir and Lord: one Greek word
p: Greek kyria is 'lady'; its masculine kyrios is 'sir' to a man and 'Lord' for God.
b: Hermas calls Rhoda, and then the old woman, kyria, a polite 'lady' or 'madam'. Its masculine, kyrios, is what he calls the young man of 18:9 ('Sir'), and also the word for God and Christ, 'the Lord', all through the book. Greek readers heard one word where English needs three. The Plain English Translation uses 'lady' and 'sir' in address and 'the Lord' for God, following the sense, as the site does in the Gospels ('sir' when a stranger speaks to Jesus). Where it is not clear whom kyrios means, a note says so.

a: to bring your sins to light before the Lord
p: Rhoda has been 'taken up' to heaven to expose Hermas: is she dead, or is this only a vision?
b: The verb anelēmphthēn ('I was taken up') is the word used for Jesus' going up into heaven (Acts 1:2). It could mean that Rhoda had died; the text does not say, and Hermas speaks of her afterward as 'a very good woman' (2:3), as of someone living. Her role is that of a witness in God's court. In the Bible the accuser in heaven is the satan (Zechariah 3:1; Revelation 12:10), but Rhoda is not hostile: she denies that she is his accuser (1:6) and only reports God's anger.

a: created from nothing the things that are
p: Hermas says plainly that God made the things that are out of what is not.
b: The Greek ktisas ek tou mē ontos ta onta, 'having created, out of what is not, the things that are', echoes the mother's words in 2 Maccabees 7:28, 'God made them, not from things that were', and Paul's God who 'calls the things that are not as though they were' (Romans 4:17). Mandate 1 repeats the thought (26:1). Lake's margin gives Psalm 2:4 and Psalm 123:1 for 'who lives in heaven' and Genesis 1:28 for 'multiplied them and made them grow'.
orig: κτίσας ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος τὰ ὄντα

a: for the sake of his holy church
t: The world made for the Church
p: From the first page the world exists for the sake of the Church, a theme 8:1 states outright.
b: God multiplied creation 'for the sake of his holy church'. In 8:1 the young man adds that the Church 'was created first of all' and that 'the world was put in order for her sake', and the hymn of 3:4 puts the creation of the world and of the church side by side. Hermas gives the Church the place of God's first purpose. The chapter page of 8 takes up how this has been read.

a: The desire for wickedness rose up in your heart
p: Rhoda's charge stands close to Jesus' word about looking with desire in Matthew 5:28.
b: Hermas only thought of having a wife like Rhoda, yet she calls it 'a sin, and a great one'. The point is the same as Jesus' saying, 'anyone who looks at a woman so as to lust after her has, in his heart, already committed adultery with her' (Matthew 5:28), though Hermas does not quote it. The Greek idiom 'went up upon your heart' (Hebrew-style, as in Jeremiah 3:16, 'come to mind') means 'entered your thoughts'. The old woman later softens the charge: God is angry 'not because of this' but because of Hermas's household (3:1).

a: make this world their own
p: The Greek here is aiōn, 'age', the present world-order that passes away.
b: Hermas uses ho aiōn houtos, 'this age', for the present world and its riches (also 14:5-6), and kosmos for the world itself (8:1; 24:2). The Plain English Translation says 'this world' for the first, as Lake does, because English 'this age' does not carry the sense of property and getting ahead that the verb peripoioumenoi ('acquiring for themselves') gives here. The contrast is 'the age that is coming' (24:5).

a: Their souls will repent
p: The verb is the book's key word, 'repent', used here of a repentance that comes with no hope.
b: The Greek is metanoēsousin, 'they will repent', from metanoia, 'repentance' (gloss: 'turn your life around'), the word the whole Shepherd turns on. Here it is a repentance without hope, as the next words say ('they have no hope'): the sense may be a regret that comes too late, or a turning that is still open, since the verse goes on at once to 'pray to God, and he will heal'. The Plain English Translation keeps 'repent', as Lake does ('Their hearts will repent; yet have they no hope'), so that the book's key word reads the same everywhere. The angel who gives the book its name is 'the angel of repentance' (25). Lake's margin points to Deuteronomy 30:3 and Jeremiah 3:22 for the healing that follows.

a: If even this sin is written down against me
p: Hermas fears his sin is entered in God's record, as the Bible pictures books in heaven.
b: The Greek anagraphetai is 'is written down'. Hebrew and Christian writers pictured heavenly books of deeds (Daniel 7:10; Revelation 20:12), as well as the book of life (3:2). Hermas's question, 'how can I be saved?', and his worry over words to win God's mercy, show a believer who already belongs to the church and fears he has lost his place. That is the problem of the whole book: sin after baptism.

a: a large white chair, made of wool as white as snow
p: The old woman's chair is a teacher's seat; in 19:4 it becomes a sign of weakness.
b: A kathedra was the chair a teacher sat in, the word behind English 'cathedral', the church of a bishop's chair. White wool like snow recalls the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7:9 ('the hair of his head was like clean wool') and Christ in Revelation 1:14. The young man explains in 19:4 that she sat 'because everyone who is weak sits in a chair'. So the chair works both ways: a seat of honor and teaching, and a sign of a church grown old and weary.

a: An old woman came
p: She is not named until 8:1, where she is revealed to be the Church.
b: Here the Greek is gynē presbytis, 'an old woman'; from 5:3 she is hē presbytera, 'the old one', a word that also means 'elder' (see 8:1). Hermas does not yet know who she is and later guesses she is the Sibyl (8:1). She wears shining clothes and holds a book, like a heavenly messenger. Over the Visions she grows younger (18:3-5; 23:1), and the chapter pages of 8 and 18-21 explain why.

a: patient and slow to take offense
p: The woman describes Hermas by two virtues the Mandates later teach: patience and calm.
b: Makrothymos is 'patient' (the virtue of Mandate 5, 33-34) and astomachētos 'slow to take offense'. With 'always laughing' and 'cheerful' (hilaros), the woman draws a man known for good humor. Cheerfulness is a virtue in this book (42 is on grief and cheerfulness), and the woman herself grows more cheerful as the visions go on (18:4-5).

a: a slave of God
p: Greek doulos is 'slave'; Hermas, a former slave, calls believers God's slaves all through the book.
b: The site renders doulos 'slave', as in Jude 1:1, because the Greek means a person owned by another, not a hired servant. Many English Bibles say 'servant' to soften it. For a writer who had himself been sold (1:1), the title 'slave of God' is not a figure of speech worn lightly: it means belonging wholly to a new master. Hermas uses it for every believer (22:3, 'his slaves who had stumbled'), and the parable of Similitude 5 (55) is about a slave.
orig: ὁ δοῦλος τοῦ θεοῦ (ho doulos tou theou)

a: a spirit so revered, one already tested
p: The old woman's words describe Hermas as a baptized believer, already proved.
b: She calls Hermas's spirit pansemnon, 'worthy of all reverence' (Lake: 'a revered spirit'), the same family of words as Reverence, one of the seven women (16:5), and ēdē dedokimasmenon, 'already tested'. The words fit someone baptized and proved in the faith. For such a person, she says, even an evil plan in the heart brings sin. Lake's introduction says the circle Hermas belonged to believed that 'Christians after baptism were capable of leading sinless lives'. Hermas the 'self-controlled', full of 'simplicity and great innocence', is held up to that standard, and the book goes on to ask what happens when believers fall short of it.

a: You love your children too much
t: A father who did not correct his children
p: Hermas's fault is the fault of Eli, who did not hold his sons back.
b: The Greek philoteknos is 'child-loving', a virtue in Titus 2:4, here pushed too far: Hermas did not 'correct' (nouthetein, 'warn, set right') his household. God's word against Eli is similar: 'His sons were cursing God, and he did not hold them back' (1 Samuel 3:13). The cure the woman gives is daily words (3:2), not violence.

a: the business of everyday life
p: Hermas has been 'ruined by the business of everyday life', a theme of the whole book.
b: The Greek biōtikai praxeis, 'the affairs of ordinary living', is close to the phrase the site renders 'the business of everyday life' in 2 Timothy 2:4. The verb katephtharēs is 'you were ruined' (Lake: 'corrupted'), the same verb as 'you let it go to ruin' earlier in the verse. Hermas returns to the theme: he had been rich (14:7), got 'tangled up' in his business (7:1), and the believers whom the woman calls weak have been 'weakened by the business of everyday life' (19:3). Business and wealth that crowd out faith run through the Visions to the round stones of 14:5-6.

a: the books of life
p: The plural 'books of life' is unusual; the Bible usually speaks of one book of life.
b: If Hermas's children repent with all their heart, they 'will be written in the books of life with the saints'. The Bible speaks of 'the book of life' (Philippians 4:3; Revelation 3:5; 20:12, where 'books' are opened and also 'the book of life'). Hermas's plural may join the two pictures. 'The saints' (gloss: 'God's holy people') are the believers.

a: All the words were terrifying, more than a person can bear
p: Like Paul in Paradise, Hermas hears what he cannot keep or repeat.
b: Hermas forgets most of the reading, 'terrifying' words 'a person cannot bear', and remembers only the gentle ending (3:4). Paul says of his own vision that he 'heard unspeakable words, words no human being is allowed to say' (2 Corinthians 12:4). 4:2 explains the difference: the hard words were for the nations and the deserters, the gentle ones for the righteous.

a: set the earth firm on the waters
p: The old woman's reading sounds like a psalm: God fixed the sky and founded the earth on the waters.
b: The lines echo the Psalms: God 'laid its base upon the seas' (Psalm 24:2) and 'stretched the earth flat on top of the waters' (Psalm 136:6). Lake's margin gives 'Ps. 135, 6'; the verse about the earth on the waters is the site's Psalm 136:6, not its Psalm 135:6. The same order runs from creation to the church: by his power God made the world, by his word he fixed the sky, and 'by his own wisdom and care he created his holy church'. The earth on the waters prepares the tower on the waters (10:4; 11:5).

a: everything is becoming level ground for his chosen
p: God moves heavens, mountains, hills and seas to make a level way for his chosen people.
b: Isaiah's voice cries that 'each mountain and hill sink low' to prepare the way for God (Isaiah 40:4), and Revelation sees mountains and islands moved and the sky rolled up (Revelation 6:14). Hermas turns the picture into comfort: the end is a road made smooth for 'his chosen' (Greek eklektoi, the site's word in Matthew 24:31), who will receive the promise 'if they keep God's rules'. The 'if' is the Shepherd's whole message.

a: went off with it toward the east
p: The chair and the woman go to the east, the direction of paradise and of God's glory.
b: God planted the garden 'in Eden, in the east' (Genesis 2:8), and Ezekiel saw God's glory coming back 'from the way of the east' (Ezekiel 43:2). Hermas does not explain the direction, but four young men (angels: see 12:1) carry the chair and two men lead the woman away to the same place, as servants carry a great lady.

a: for the nations and for those who have turned away from the faith
p: Greek ethnē, 'nations', means the peoples who are not God's people: here, those outside the church.
b: In the Bible ta ethnē are the nations, the Gentiles, as against Israel. In Hermas they are the heathen, those not baptized, as in 6:5 ('for the nations there is repentance until the last day'). Lake's English there says 'the heathen'. The apostatai are deserters, believers who turned their backs on the faith. The hard words of the reading are for them; the gentle ones 'for the righteous'.

a: Be brave, Hermas!
p: Greek andrizou is 'act like a man', the word Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 16:13.
b: Andrizou, from anēr, 'man', means 'be brave, show courage'. Paul's 'Show courage' (1 Corinthians 16:13) is the same verb, and the Greek of Joshua 1:6 has the same command, ischye kai andrizou. Self-control in 16:4 is 'standing strong like a man' with the same word, and the old man in 20:2 'acts like a man' when new strength comes. The cheerful farewell after the hard reading is the first sign of the woman's turn toward hope.

a: at the same season as the year before
t: A year later, on the same road
p: The second vision comes a year after the first, at the same time and on the same road.
b: Hermas ties his visions to dates and places: a year passes between the first two visions (5:1; 18:3 'last year'), fifteen days of fasting before the meaning of the book is given (6:1), and twenty days before the fourth vision (22:1). Whether these are real events, a literary frame, or both is part of the question of how the book was written (the historical lens on the book's opening pages). The road to Cumae is the same as in 1:3; see the variant there for the place name.

a: a little book
p: The old woman's little book is like the little scroll John is handed in Revelation 10.
b: The Greek biblaridion (and biblidion), 'a little book', is the word Revelation 10:2 and 10:9-10 use for the little scroll the angel holds and John eats. Hermas is not told to eat his book, but to copy it, announce it, and later to make two copies (8:3). The contents are given in 6:2-7:4: a message to Hermas's family and to the whole church. A prophet receiving a written book from heaven is an old picture (Ezekiel 2:9-3:3).

a: letter by letter, because I could not make out where the syllables broke
p: Hermas copied the book one letter at a time because, like old manuscripts, it ran on without spaces.
b: Lake's footnote: 'Hermas no doubt means that it was written, like most early MSS., in a continuous script with no divisions between the words.' Greek books of the time were written in capitals with no spaces, and readers sounded the letters out in syllables to find the words. Hermas could not, so he copied blind, and the meaning came only after fifteen days of fasting and prayer (6:1). The scene makes the message a gift: he copied what he did not yet understand.

a: after I had fasted and begged the Lord again and again
p: Hermas fasts to receive the meaning of the book, as Daniel fasted before his visions.
b: Daniel mourned and ate no rich food for three weeks before the vision of Daniel 10, and fasted when he sought to understand Jeremiah's seventy years (Daniel 9:3). Hermas fasts 'many times' before Vision 3 (9:2) and for one day in 18:6-7, where an angel warns him not to harm his body by asking so much. The Similitudes later teach a fast whose savings go to the poor (54-56).

a: your children
p: The Greek is 'your seed', a Hebrew way of saying 'your children'.
b: To sperma sou, 'your seed', is singular with a plural verb ('they rejected'), a Hebrew idiom for one's offspring (Genesis 15:5). The Plain English Translation says 'your children'. The charges are heavy: they rejected God, blasphemed the Lord, betrayed their parents. How they betrayed their parents the text does not say; 6:7-8 speak of persecution and denial, which may be the setting, and the old woman promises forgiveness if they repent (6:4).

a: your wife, who is going to be your sister
t: A wife who will be a sister
p: Hermas's wife is to become his 'sister'; the text does not say whether this means a marriage lived without sex or a sister in the faith.
b: Lake's English renders it 'your wife, who shall in future be to you as a sister'. It may mean that the two are to live together from now on without sex, as brother and sister, or that she is to become his 'sister' in the faith by repenting; the text gives no reason, and 7:1 calls her simply 'your sister'. Paul allows a married couple to abstain for a time by agreement, for prayer (1 Corinthians 7:5). Her fault here is her tongue.

a: all the saints who have sinned up to this day
p: Forgiveness is offered for every sin committed up to the day of the revelation.
b: This is the heart of Vision 2. Sins committed 'up to this day' will be forgiven if the sinners repent with all their heart and drive out double-mindedness (Greek dipsychia; see 6:7). The offer is for 'the saints', the baptized. 6:5 adds that there is no second chance after this. The chapter page of 6 lays out how this offer has been read.

a: The days of repentance are over for all the saints
p: Lake: 'This is the main point of the Shepherd.' The baptized get one more chance, and only one.
b: Lake's footnote: 'The primitive teaching was that for sin after baptism no repentance is possible (cf. Heb. vi.). Hermas now states that it has been revealed to him that "up to this day", i.e. the time of his revelation, sin will be forgiven to the repentant. But this offer of forgiveness will not be made a second time.' Hebrews 6:4-6 says it is 'impossible' to bring back to repentance those who once received the light and fell away. Hermas opens a door once, with a deadline, while for 'the nations' repentance stays open to the end. Mandate 4 states the rule again: 'one repentance' (31:6).

a: the Master has sworn by his own glory
p: God swears by his glory, as Hebrews says he swore by himself to Abraham.
b: God, the despotēs ('Master', the site's word for despotēs of God), takes an oath. Hebrews explains God's oath to Abraham: 'He could not swear by anyone greater, so he swore an oath by himself' (Hebrews 6:13). In 6:8 'the Lord has sworn by his Son'. An oath makes the deadline unchangeable, which is why so much of the later book (Mandate 4, the Similitudes) works out what the promise means for those who still sin.

a: the leaders of the church
p: Greek proēgoumenoi, 'those who go before', a general word for leaders, beside 'elders' in 8:2-3.
b: The Visions use several words for those in charge: proēgoumenoi here and in 17:7, 'the elders who lead the church' (8:3), the 'front seats' (17:7), and in 13:1 'apostles and overseers and teachers and deacons'. Hebrews uses a close word for the church's 'leaders' who must 'give an account' (Hebrews 13:17), and Hermas's woman says she must give an account for her children (17:10). The text shows a group of leaders in Rome, named as a body; it never names one head over the others.

a: do not be double-minded
p: Greek dipsychos, 'two-souled', is Hermas's favorite word for wavering faith (gloss: of two minds).
b: Dipsychos, 'double-minded', the noun dipsychia and the verb dipsychein stand 58 times in Lake's Greek of the Shepherd (a count by script). In the New Testament the word is James's: 'He is a double-minded man, never steady on any road he takes' (James 1:8; also James 4:8). In Hermas it means doubt that God will keep his promises, faith divided between God and the world (11:4; 12:3; 22:4). Mandate 9 is wholly about it (39).

a: your passing may be with the holy angels
p: Lake points to Similitude 9.25 and the Martyrdom of Polycarp for the righteous becoming like angels.
b: The Greek parodos is a 'passing' (Lake: 'that your passing may be with the holy angels'). Lake's footnote compares Similitude 9.25 (102) and the Martyrdom of Polycarp 2:3, 'with the note on the latter passage as to the doctrine of a transformation of the just into angels after their death.' Jesus says the risen 'are like angels in heaven' (Mark 12:25). Hermas promises those who stand firm that their passing will be in the company of the holy angels; he does not say more about where it leads.
r: Mark 12:25; Luke 20:36; Martyrdom of Polycarp 2:3; Hebrews 12:22-23

a: Blessed are you, all who endure the great suffering that is coming
p: A beatitude for those who endure a coming persecution, close to James 1:12 and Revelation 7:14.
b: James says 'Blessed is the man who endures through trial' (James 1:12), and Revelation sees 'the ones who are coming out of the great suffering' (Revelation 7:14). The Greek thlipsis (gloss: 'hard times, above all persecution'; Lake 'persecution') is the same word. Hermas expects a persecution soon (7:4; 23:5; 24:6). Those 'who will not deny their life' are those who will not deny Christ, who is their life; 6:8 says so.

a: the Lord has sworn by his Son
p: Hermas speaks of God's Son here; he never uses the names Jesus or Christ except in the variant of this verse.
b: God swears 'by his Son' that those who deny 'their Christ' are cut off from their life. In Lake's Greek and Latin the names 'Jesus' and 'Christ' occur nowhere else in the Shepherd: the book speaks of 'the Son of God', 'the Lord' and 'the Name'. Even here the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus reads 'Christ' and the other witnesses 'Lord' or 'Son' (see the variant). Those who denied him 'before', in earlier persecutions, are forgiven; those who deny him in the days to come will not be. Jesus warns, 'whoever denies me in front of people, I too will deny' (Matthew 10:33).

a: stop holding a grudge against your children
p: Greek mnēsikakein is 'to remember wrongs': keeping score against someone.
b: Mnēsikakeō means to remember the evil done to you and hold it against the one who did it. Hermas's children had wronged him (6:2), and he is told to let it go, for 'holding a grudge brings death'. Mandate 9 and Similitude 9 return to the vice. Proverbs (in the Greek) and Zechariah warn against it, and Jesus ties God's forgiveness to ours (Matthew 6:14-15).

a: you did not turn away from the living God
t: Not turning away from the living God
p: Hebrews 3:12 has the same verb: 'the kind that deserts the living God'.
b: Lake's margin gives Hebrews 3:12 here and again at 15:2. Hebrews warns against 'a wicked heart of unbelief, the kind that deserts the living God' (Hebrews 3:12). The Greek verb in both is aphistēmi, 'stand away from', the word behind 'apostasy'. Hermas had sinned and neglected his household, but he had not deserted God. Those who 'have turned away from the living God for good' are the stones that fall into the fire (15:2). Simplicity and self-control, two of the seven women of 16:5, are what save him.

a: Blessed are all who do what is right
p: Lake's margin gives Psalm 106:3; Hermas's Greek follows the Greek Psalm, not the site's Hebrew wording.
b: The site's Psalm 106:3, from the Hebrew, says 'Happy are those who hold to justice, the one who does what is right in every season'. The Greek Psalm (105:3 in Swete) blesses those 'doing righteousness' (poiountes dikaiosynēn), and Hermas's hoi ergazomenoi tēn dikaiosynēn, 'those who work righteousness', is the very phrase of the Greek Psalm 14:2 (the site's Psalm 15:2), which Lake also lists. The Plain English Translation renders Hermas's own words.

a: Maximus
p: Someone in Hermas's church, otherwise unknown; 'deny again' implies that he had denied before.
b: Nothing else is known of Maximus. The words are 'Look, suffering is coming. If you think it best, deny again' (Greek ean soi phanē, palin arnēsai, a command). Lake's English adds 'the faith' ('deny the faith again'). The word 'again' implies that Maximus had denied once before. The command can be read as irony, a sharp way of saying 'do not', or as a bitter permission; the text does not explain it, and Lake's footnote is only on the names that follow. The saying that comes next ('The Lord is near to those who turn back') holds out hope to someone who turns back, and 6:8 has already said that the Lord has been merciful to those who denied before.

a: as it is written in
p: Hermas quotes no book of the Bible by name; the one written source he names is the lost Book of Eldad and Modad.
b: 'As it is written' (hōs gegraptai) is the formula the New Testament uses for Scripture, and here it introduces a saying from the Book of Eldad and Modad (the Greek here spells the second name 'Modat'; Numbers 11:26 has Medad), a prophecy named after the two men who prophesied in the camp (Numbers 11:26). Lake's footnote: 'This book is mentioned among the Apocrypha of the N.T. in the Athanasian Synopsis and in the Stichometry of Nicephorus, but is not extant. It is thought to be quoted in II Clem. xi. 2.' The saying itself, 'The Lord is near to those who turn back', is close to Psalm 145:18 ('Near is the LORD to everyone who calls to him'). The quotation shows Hermas's church reading a book that is in no Bible today.

a: a very handsome young man
p: Young men in this book are angels, as the young man at the tomb is in Mark 16:5.
b: The six young men who build the tower are 'the holy angels of God who were created first' (12:1), and the young man of 18:7 explains the visions. Angels in human form are young men in Mark 16:5 ('a young man sitting on the right, clothed in a long white robe') and 2 Maccabees 3:26. This one corrects Hermas's guess about the old woman.

a: The Sibyl
p: Hermas first takes the old woman for the Sibyl, the aged prophetess of Greek and Roman legend.
b: Cumae, the place Hermas was walking toward when the visions began (1:3; 5:1), was a Greek colony near Naples and the seat of the Cumaean Sibyl, the priestess of Apollo's oracle there. In the Roman story the Sibylline Books were bought by King Tarquinius Superbus and kept in the Temple of Jupiter on the Capitoline Hill, to be consulted only in emergencies. An old woman with a book of prophecy met on the road to Cumae would make a Roman think of her. Jewish and Christian writers also wrote oracles in the Sibyl's name (the Sibylline Oracles). The young man says Hermas is wrong: she is the Church. Hermas borrows the Sibyl's picture and gives it a new meaning, a pagan image put to Christian use.

a: The old woman you got the little book from
p: Greek presbytera is 'the older woman', the feminine of presbyteros, 'elder'.
b: From 5:3 the woman is called hē presbytera, 'the old one'. The same word, in the masculine, is the title of the church's elders, presbyteroi, who appear in the next verse (8:2) and in 8:3 and 9:8. The Plain English Translation keeps 'the old woman', but a Greek reader heard the link: the Church herself is 'the elder', older than the world. In 1 Timothy 5:2 presbyterai means simply 'older women'.

a: she was created first of all
p: The Church existed before the world, and the world was made for her: the pre-existent Church.
b: The young man explains her age: she 'was created first of all', and 'the world was put in order for her sake'. 2 Clement says the same: 'the first church, the spiritual one, which was created before the sun and moon' (2 Clement 14:1). Paul says God 'chose us in Christ before the world was founded' (Ephesians 1:4) and calls 'the Jerusalem above' 'our mother' (Galatians 4:26). The chapter page of 8 sets the readings side by side, and 19:2 gives a second reason for her age.

a: if I had already given the book to the elders
p: The church in Rome is led by elders, a group, with no single head named.
b: Presbyteroi, 'elders', is the office of 1 Timothy 5:17 ('Elders who lead well should be counted worthy of a double honor'). In 8:3 the old woman calls them 'the elders who lead the church' (proistamenoi, the verb of 1 Timothy 5:17 and 1 Thessalonians 5:12). Hermas is not one of them: he reads the book 'with' them. The Visions name only elders and leaders in the plural; whether Rome also had a single overseer at this time they do not say. The site's cards on bishops and elders (1 Timothy 3; Titus 1) give the churches' views.

a: one to Clement
p: Clement's task is to send writings to 'the cities abroad', which fits the Clement of 1 Clement.
b: The woman orders one copy 'to Clement', who will send it 'to the cities abroad, for that is the task given to him'. The letter called 1 Clement was sent from the church in Rome to Corinth, and tradition names Clement as its writer. Lake (introduction to 1 Clement): this 'certainly points to a Clement in Rome exercising the same functions as the writer of I. Clement; but Hermas is probably somewhat later than I. Clement, and the reference may be merely a literary device based on knowledge of the earlier book.' If the Clement is the living man, the Visions are older than the Muratorian list's date under Pius (Lake: about 148). The book's opening pages weigh the options.

a: Grapte will instruct the widows and the orphans
p: A woman, otherwise unknown, with a teaching task among the church's widows and orphans.
b: Grapte is named only here. The verb nouthetēsei is 'will warn, instruct', the word used of Hermas correcting his family (3:2). The church in Rome cared for widows and orphans as James says true religion does: 'to visit orphans and widows in their trouble' (James 1:27). Whether this was an office for women, like the enrolled widows of 1 Timothy 5:9-10 or the deacon Phoebe (Romans 16:1), the text does not say: it names only the task. Her copy shows that the book was meant for the whole church, not only its leaders.

a: the field where you farm
p: Hermas is sent to 'the field where you farm'; the Greek verb is rare, and the Plain English Translation follows Lake.
b: The verb chondrizeis is rare. Lake translates 'come into the country, where you are farming', and the Plain English Translation follows his sense. The book does not say whether the field is Hermas's own or one he works for someone else. He is told to come at about the fifth hour (gloss: 'about eleven in the morning').

a: an ivory couch
t: The ivory couch and the linen
p: A costly ivory couch with linen cushion and cloth: a seat for a rich Roman household, set in a field.
b: Lake's index calls it 'Couch of ivory'. The Greek has a couch (sympselion), a linen cushion (kerbikarion) and a cloth of fine linen (lention ... karpasion). The couch is set ready like a seat for a meeting, before anyone arrives. The woman sits on it to show the tower (10:4), and in 21:3 its four legs become a sign of a firm footing, like the world's four elements.

a: my hair stood on end
p: Hermas's terror at the empty place echoes Eliphaz's night vision in Job.
b: 'A breath of wind slid past my face, and the hair of my skin bristled' (Job 4:15). Hermas trembles and shudders 'because I was alone', then 'came to himself', remembered God's glory, and prayed. Fear followed by courage is the pattern of the Visions; the beast of Vision 4 tests it again (22:7-8).

a: let the elders sit first
p: Hermas defers to 'the elders': the church's leaders, or just 'older people first'?
b: Lake's footnote: 'The meaning is obscure: "the elders" is often explained as "the Elders of the Church", but it is more probably a mere formula of politeness "seniores priores"', that is, 'older people first'. The Greek presbyteroi can mean either. If Hermas means the church's elders, he thinks they should be given the first seats in the vision as they are in church; the woman's sharp 'sit down' and her later warning to 'you who take the front seats' (17:7) would then have an edge.

a: The place on the right belongs to others
t: The right side and the left
p: The right-hand seats go to those who have suffered for the Name, as Jesus said the right was not his to give.
b: James and John asked to sit at Jesus' right and left; he answered, 'the seats at my right and my left are not mine to hand out' (Matthew 20:23). Hermas is not allowed the right side, which belongs to 'those who have already pleased God and have suffered for the sake of the Name'. 10:1 explains: both sides have 'the same gifts and the same promises'; those on the right only 'have a certain glory'. The martyrs are honored above others, but they are not saved by a different gift.

a: for the sake of the Name
p: 'The Name' standing alone means Christ's name, as in Acts 5:41 and 3 John 7.
b: Early Christians spoke of suffering 'for the sake of the Name' without saying whose: the apostles were 'glad at heart, because they had been found worthy to be dishonored for the sake of the Name' (Acts 5:41; also 3 John 1:7). Hermas does the same (10:1; 13:2 'the name of the Lord'; 23:4 'the great and glorious Name'). In 11:5 the tower is founded 'by the word of the almighty and glorious Name'. The witnesses differ over whose name is meant here (see the variant).

a: Whips, prisons, great sufferings, crosses, and wild beasts
p: The list names punishments: flogging, prison, crosses and being thrown to wild beasts.
b: Hebrews remembers believers who 'went through jeering and lashes, and besides that, chains and prison' (Hebrews 11:36), and being given to the beasts was the death Ignatius expected in Rome (Ignatius to the Romans 4:1). Hermas does not name a persecution or an emperor. 'The holy place' is hagiasma, a sanctuary: the scene is a heavenly court with seats on both sides.
r: Hebrews 11:36-37; 2 Corinthians 11:23-25; Ignatius to the Romans 4:1; 1 Corinthians 15:32

a: a great tower being built on the water
p: The tower is the Church (11:3), built on water (baptism, 11:5) from stones that are believers.
b: The woman explains it herself: 'The tower that you see being built is I myself, the Church' (11:3), built on water 'because your life was saved through water' (11:5). The picture is Paul's and Peter's: the church 'is growing up as a temple' (Ephesians 2:21), believers are 'stones that live' built 'into a spiritual house' (1 Peter 2:5). Hermas tells the tower twice: here in Vision 3 (10-15), and again in Similitude 9 (78-110), where it stands on a great white rock with a gate, both of which are the Son of God (79:1-2; 89:1), in a plain ringed by twelve mountains (78:4), and the stones are handed in by virgins (90:4). Here there is no rock and no gate: the tower rests on the waters, held up by seven women (16:2). In 1 Enoch's Animal Apocalypse a 'high tower' stands for God's house (1 Enoch 89:50); the Tower of Babel is the Bible's tower of pride (Genesis 11:4).
r: Ephesians 2:20-22; 1 Peter 2:4-5; 1 Corinthians 3:9-15; Matthew 16:18; Genesis 11:4; 1 Enoch 89:50

a: as if it were made from a single stone
p: The stones from the deep fit so well that the tower looks like a single stone: the unity of the Church.
b: The perfect joints are the leaders and martyrs who 'always agreed with one another' (13:1-2). Solomon's temple was built of stone 'made ready at the quarry', so that no tool was heard (1 Kings 6:7), and Hermas's stones from the deep likewise need no cutting. The picture returns in Similitude 9, where the tower is built 'as if it were made from a single stone' (86:7) and becomes 'one single stone with the rock' (90:5).

a: Some of them were scabby
p: Greek epsōriakotes, 'having the itch', is a skin disease word used of stones with rough, eaten surfaces.
b: Psōriaō means to have psōra, an itching rash or mange. Hermas uses it of stones with a rough, flaking face. In 14:2 these are 'those who have known the truth but did not stay in it'. The four kinds of unused stones here (scabby, cracked, cut short, white and round) are each explained in 14:2-6.

a: the parables of the tower
p: Greek parabolē, 'parable', is the book's word for a picture that needs explaining.
b: The woman calls the parts of the vision parabolai, 'parables', the Gospels' word for Jesus' stories. The last division of the book is called the Parables (Lake's English) or, from the Latin, the Similitudes (50-114). In the Visions the word means a sign to be decoded: each part of the tower stands for something, and the woman explains them in 11-15.

a: because you have no shame
p: The woman calls Hermas shameless for his endless questions, the word of Jesus' parable of the friend at midnight.
b: Anaidēs, 'shameless', is a rebuke with a smile. Jesus praises the same quality in the friend who knocks at midnight: 'he will get up because of his shamelessness and give him whatever he needs' (Luke 11:8, Greek anaideia). Hermas describes himself the same way in 15:5 ('Still shameless, I asked her more'). The book's humor at Hermas's expense (11:1 'a sly man'; 14:5 'foolish and senseless') is part of its charm.

a: is I myself, the Church
p: The woman says she is the tower: the Church is both a person who speaks and a building in progress.
b: The same Church appears as a woman who teaches and as a tower being built. The two pictures say different things: the woman is the Church as a mother who raises children (17:1), the tower is the Church as made up of believers, still being built until the end (16:9). Paul mixes pictures in the same way: the church is a body, a temple and a bride (1 Corinthians 12:27; Ephesians 2:21; 5:25-27).

a: Whatever can be revealed to you will be revealed
p: Clement of Alexandria quotes this line from Hermas's vision as a revelation.
b: In his Stromata (book 2, chapter 1, in the Ante-Nicene Fathers translation) Clement writes: 'For the power that appeared in the vision to Hermas said, Whatever may be revealed to you, shall be revealed.' Clement quotes the Shepherd several times in that book (also 16:3 below), treating it as a work that speaks with authority. The book's opening pages take up how far the early churches counted it as Scripture.

a: your life was saved through water
p: The tower stands on water because life is saved through water: baptism.
b: Hermas does not use the word 'baptism' here, but 15:3 speaks of those who 'wanted to be baptized in the name of the Lord' and could not roll into the water. 1 Peter makes the same link: Noah's family 'were carried safe through water', and 'baptism, the counterpart of that water, saves you now as well' (1 Peter 3:20-21). The tower 'was saved and will be saved' through water. How baptism saves is a question the churches answer differently; see the site's cards on baptism at Acts 2, Mark 16 and Romans 6.

a: the holy angels of God who were created first
p: Six chief angels build the tower; Jewish writings speak of seven chief angels.
b: Tobit has Raphael as 'one of the seven angels who stand in attendance and go in before the glory of the Lord' (Tobit 12:15), and 1 Enoch 20 lists seven 'holy angels who keep watch': Uriel, Raphael, Raguel, Michael, Saraqael, Gabriel and Remiel. Hermas has six, with countless lesser angels under them (12:2). In Similitude 9 six men are 'the glorious angels who support him on his right and on his left', beside 'the glorious man', who is the Son of God (89:8). The six were given creation 'to make it grow, to build it up, and to rule over all of it'.

a: what their power means
p: Greek dynamis is 'power'; Lake says here it is 'almost the equivalent of meaning'.
b: Hermas asks about the stones' exodos ('outcome', what becomes of them) and their dynamis, 'power'. Lake's footnote: 'Here almost the equivalent of "meaning." "What is their meaning in the vision?"' He says the same of the women's 'powers' in 16:6. The Plain English Translation keeps the word and shows the sense.

a: It is for the sake of the double-minded
p: Hermas is not shown these things because he is the best, but for those who doubt.
b: The woman deflates Hermas: others are 'ahead of you and better than you'. The visions are for 'the double-minded, who argue in their hearts over whether these things are so or not', that is, believers who doubt that the promises and the judgment are real. That is one reason the book is so full of explanations: it aims to reassure.

a: apostles and overseers and teachers and deacons
p: The best stones are four kinds of ministers. 'Overseer' (Greek episkopos) is the word behind 'bishop'.
b: The square white stones are 'apostles and overseers and teachers and deacons'. Episkopos, 'overseer' (gloss: the word behind 'bishop'), and diakonos, 'deacon', are the officers of Philippians 1:1 ('overseers and deacons'). Apostles and teachers are among Christ's gifts in Ephesians 4:11 and 1 Corinthians 12:28. The verbs follow: they 'watched over' (episkopēsantes), 'taught' and 'served'. 'Some of them have fallen asleep, and some are still living': the clause covers all four groups, so it does not say which of them, apostles included, were dead when Hermas wrote. The list does not rank them or say whether 'overseers' and 'elders' are the same people; the site's cards on bishops and elders (1 Timothy 3; Titus 1) give the churches' views.
orig: ἀπόστολοι καὶ ἐπίσκοποι καὶ διδάσκαλοι καὶ διάκονοι

a: without being cut
p: Greek latomeō, 'cut stone at the quarry': the best believers need no trimming to fit.
b: Some stones from the dry land go in without being cut, 'because they walked in the Lord's straight way'. Others need trimming, and the round stones need their wealth 'cut away' (14:6). The picture recalls the temple stones 'made ready at the quarry' (1 Kings 6:7). Cutting stands for the discipline and suffering that shape a believer to fit the building.

a: if they repent now, while the tower is being built
t: While the tower is being built
p: Repentance has a deadline: the finishing of the tower, that is, the end.
b: The stones set aside are those 'who have sinned and want to repent'. They lie near the tower and will be used if they repent 'now'. 'Once the building is finished, they no longer have a place.' The same time limit runs through the Visions (6:5; 16:9; 17:5). In Similitude 9 the building has a pause, 'so that if these people repent, they may go into the building of the tower' (82:1; 91:2).

a: These are the children of lawlessness
p: 'Sons of lawlessness' is a Hebrew way of saying 'lawless people', like Paul's 'man of lawlessness'.
b: Hoi huioi tēs anomias, 'the sons of lawlessness', describes people by what they belong to, as 'sons of disobedience' (Ephesians 2:2) or 'the son of ruin' (2 Thessalonians 2:3; the same verse has 'the man of lawlessness'). They 'believed, but in pretense' (en hypokrisei), and kept every wickedness. They are thrown far away 'because of the Lord's anger'. Unlike the stones set aside nearby (13:5), there is no word of repentance for them here, though 15:5 opens a narrow door.

a: the white round ones that do not fit into the building
p: Round stones cannot be built into a square tower until their wealth is trimmed away.
b: The white round stones are believers who 'also have the wealth of this world', who deny their Lord in persecution 'because of their wealth and their business dealings'. In the parable of the sower, 'the worries of the age and the trickery of wealth choke the message' (Matthew 13:22). A round stone must be trimmed to become square (14:6). Hermas is not against the rich as such: in 14:7 he is himself a trimmed stone, and Similitude 2 (51) gives the rich a place in supporting the poor.

a: For you yourself are being used as one of these very stones
p: Lake says the Greek is obscure; the sense seems to be that Hermas is one of these stones, trimmed.
b: Lake's footnote on 'you yourself are taken from the same stones': 'This appears to be the meaning; but the Greek is obscure and the early translations all paraphrase it so freely that they cannot be used to suggest any emendation.' The point is clear enough: Hermas was rich and useless (compare his business in 7:1), and is now 'useful'; how his wealth was 'cut away' the verse does not say. He is the example of his own parable. The Plain English Translation reads the verb chrasai as 'you are being used'. Codex Sinaiticus lacks the sentence altogether (see the variant).
orig: καὶ γὰρ σὺ αὐτὸς χρᾶσαι ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν λίθων

a: they leave their true way
p: The double-minded wander off the road into country with no road, as James's double-minded man is 'never steady on any road'.
b: James says the double-minded man is 'never steady on any road he takes' (James 1:8). Hermas turns this into a picture: stones that land on the road roll off it into roadless country, thinking they can find 'a better way'. The two roads of Jesus' saying (Matthew 7:13-14) and the Two Ways teaching of the Didache stand behind the idea of one true way.

a: turned away from the living God for good
p: Those in the fire have turned away for good; it no longer enters their hearts to repent.
b: The Greek eis telos is 'to the end, completely'. The verb is the 'turn away' of Hebrews 3:12 (see 7:2). The fault is not that God refuses them, but that 'it no longer even enters their hearts to repent', because of their desires. This is close to Hebrews 6:4-6, where it is impossible to bring the fallen back to repentance; Hermas places the impossibility in the sinner's hardened heart (see 15:6).

a: they repent of it
p: The verb is metanoeō, 'repent', used ironically: they 'repent' of wanting to be baptized.
b: These stones heard the message and wanted to be baptized, but when they thought about 'the purity the truth demands', metanoousin, 'they repent', and go back to their desires. Lake's English keeps 'they repent'. The Plain English Translation keeps the book's key word too and adds 'of it', so the sense shows: they regret their wish, change their minds and turn back. The irony is in the Greek, where the book's word for turning to God is used for turning away. Lake's margin gives Sirach 18:30 for 'after their evil desires'.

a: They will fit into another place, a much lower one
p: The rejected stones can repent, but only for a lower place, after torment that pays off the days of their sins.
b: The woman says they 'have repentance' (15:5), but not in this tower: they will fit 'into another place, a much lower one' (Lake: 'much less honourable'), after they 'have been tormented and have served out the days of their sins'. Lake's footnote explains 'moved' as 'from their punishment', and on the next sentence: 'Apparently the meaning is "Then, i.e. if they repent," but the text is obscure, and probably some words have been lost' (see the variant). Compare Paul's builder who is saved 'like one who comes through fire' (1 Corinthians 3:15); for how the churches teach on cleansing after death, see the topic on purgatory. Hermas does not say where or when the torment takes place.

a: Do you see seven women around the tower?
p: Seven women hold up the tower: Faith and her six daughters, each a virtue born of the one before.
b: The tower 'is held up by them, by the Lord's command'. Faith is the mother; then Self-control, Simplicity, Innocence, Reverence, Understanding and Love, 'daughters of one another' (16:5, 7). Seven is the number of completeness in Jewish and Christian writing. A chain of virtues like this stands in 2 Peter 1:5-7 ('in your faith supply goodness, in goodness supply knowledge...'), which also begins with faith and ends with love. In Similitude 9 virgins stand by the tower who are 'holy spirits' and 'powers of the Son of God' (90:2).

a: is called Faith. Through her God's chosen are saved
p: Clement of Alexandria quotes this picture of Faith from 'the Shepherd'.
b: Clement writes in his Stromata (book 2, chapter 12, Ante-Nicene Fathers translation): 'The virtue, then, that encloses the Church in its grasp, as the Shepherd says, is Faith.' Faith 'with her hands clasped' (Greek kratousa tas cheiras, 'holding her hands') stands first. Paul: 'by grace you have been saved, through faith' (Ephesians 2:8).

a: dressed for action and standing strong like a man
p: Self-control is 'girded', with her clothes tucked into her belt, ready for work.
b: Periezōsmenē, 'girded', is the picture of Luke 12:35 ('Have your robes tucked into your belts') and Ephesians 6:14. Andrizomenē is the 'act like a man' of 4:3. Self-control (enkrateia, the site's word in Galatians 5:23) is Faith's first daughter, and its reward is to inherit eternal life by keeping away from every evil desire.

a: Simplicity, Understanding, Innocence, Reverence and Love
p: Each name is a Greek virtue word; the order here differs from the family tree in 16:7.
b: Haplotēs is 'simplicity' (gloss: single-heartedness, having one aim), epistēmē 'understanding' (the site's word for it in Baruch and 4 Maccabees, kept apart from synesis, 'discernment', at 3:4), akakia 'innocence' (having no evil in you), semnotēs 'reverence' (dignity, seriousness), and agapē 'love'. Here Understanding comes second; in 16:7, where they are born one from another, Understanding comes after Reverence and just before Love. Lake's text gives the two orders.

a: was it already the end?
p: Hermas asks if the end has come; the end will come when the tower is finished, and it will be built quickly.
b: The disciples asked Jesus, 'when will this happen?' (Mark 13:4) and 'is this the time?' (Acts 1:6). Hermas gets a sharper answer: 'You senseless man! Don't you see that the tower is still being built?' The end waits on the Church: when the last stone is in, the end comes. 'But it will be built up quickly.' The book lives in the expectation of a near end, and it ties the timing to the completion of God's people, as Revelation 6:11 ties it to the full number of martyrs.

a: who let righteousness fall on you drop by drop
p: The picture of righteousness falling like rain echoes Isaiah 45:8.
b: The verb stazō is 'drip'. Isaiah calls, 'Heavens, let it drip from above; clouds, let righteousness stream down' (Isaiah 45:8). The Church speaks as a mother who raised her children 'in great simplicity, innocence and reverence', three of the seven women's names (16:5). Her complaint is a mother's: you do not want to stop.

a: some bring sickness on their bodies by eating too much
p: In the same church some are sick from too much food and others from too little.
b: The Church warns that some believers 'take your share of the things God has made in heaps for yourselves alone' (17:2) while others waste away. Paul rebuked the same split at Corinth's suppers: 'one goes hungry and another gets drunk' (1 Corinthians 11:21). The word asynkrasia (17:4) is Lake's 'lack of sharing'. The cure is to share 'with those in need' (17:2, 4).

a: seek out the hungry while the tower is not yet finished
t: Do good while there is time
p: The rich must seek out the hungry now; after the tower is finished it will be too late.
b: The Church gives the same deadline for doing good as for repenting (13:5). Isaiah's true fast is to 'share your bread with the hungry' (Isaiah 58:7), and the king in Matthew 25 says 'I was hungry and you gave me food'. Those who will want to do good afterward 'will have no chance', like the young women who arrive when 'the door was closed' (Matthew 25:10).

a: their groaning may go up to the Lord
p: Lake's margin gives James 5:4: the cries of cheated workers reach the Lord's ears.
b: 'The shouts of the reapers have gone into the ears of the Lord of Armies' (James 5:4). Israel's groaning in Egypt went up to God (Exodus 2:23). The rich who ignore the needy will be 'shut out with all your goods, outside the door of the tower', their possessions with them but outside.

a: you who take the front seats
p: Greek prōtokathedritai, 'first-seat-holders', those who sit in the front seats in church.
b: The word is built on prōtokathedria, the 'front seats' Jesus says the scribes love (Matthew 23:6; Lake's margin). The Church speaks to 'you who lead the church' and to these first-seat holders together, so they are probably the leaders. Her warning is sharp: they carry poison in their hearts. 9:8 (Hermas offering the elders the first seats) may be a gentle hint of the same problem.

a: Do not be like the poisoners
p: Greek pharmakoi are drug-makers; Revelation uses the word for sorcerers.
b: Pharmakos is a maker of drugs; Revelation 21:8 uses the word for 'sorcerers'. Here the picture is of poison: poisoners keep their drugs in boxes, but the leaders keep theirs 'in your hearts'. The poison is the leaders' quarrels (17:8-9).

a: the great King
p: Lake's margin gives Psalm 47:2: 'a great King over the whole earth'.
b: God is 'a great King over the whole earth' (Psalm 47:2), and Jesus calls Jerusalem 'the city of the great King' (Matthew 5:35). Leaders who 'blend' their insight into one with a pure heart will find mercy from him.

a: give an account for all of you to the Lord
p: The Church, like the leaders of Hebrews 13:17, must give an account for those in her care.
b: Hebrews says the church's leaders watch over souls 'as people who must give an account' (Hebrews 13:17). Here the Church herself stands 'before the Father' to give account for her children, and wants to do it 'cheerful'. The witnesses differ over whether she says 'the Lord', 'our Lord' or 'your Lord' (see the variant).

a: the three forms in which she had appeared to me
p: The woman appeared old, then younger, then young: the meaning is the community's renewal.
b: Hermas lists them himself (18:3-5): very old and seated; younger in face but old in body and hair, standing; young and beautiful but with old hair, seated on a couch. The young man explains (19-21) that the forms are not about the Church's own age (as in 8:1) but about the spirit of the believers: old and weak, then renewed, then made young by repentance. In Vision 4 she appears as a young woman in white with white hair (23:1).

a: Every request needs humility. So fast
p: The old woman tells Hermas to fast; the young man warns him not to harm his body by asking too much.
b: Prayer joined to fasting was the way to ask for a revelation (6:1; Daniel 9:3). Here fasting is a sign of humility (tapeinophrosynē, as in Psalm 35:13, 'I humbled my soul with fasting'). The young man then warns Hermas that asking 'for so much' may harm his body (18:7). The book values fasting but not excess; Similitude 5 (54-56) gives its fullest teaching.

a: Sir
p: Hermas calls the young man kyrie, the same word that means 'Lord' of God (see 1:5).
b: To the young man Hermas says kyrie, the masculine of the kyria he uses for the woman. The Plain English Translation says 'sir'. In Mandates and Similitudes Hermas will say the same word to the Shepherd; there too the site says 'sir', and 'the Lord' only for God.

a: Because your spirit is old and already withered
p: The second reason for the woman's age: not that she was created first (8:1), but that your spirit is old.
b: Lake notes that 'your' here is plural, in contrast to the singular 'you' just before: the woman's age mirrors the whole community's weary spirit, 'weakness and double-mindedness'. 8:1 gave another reason: she 'was created first of all'. Both can stand: one is about what the Church is before God, the other about how she looks in a church grown tired. The young man's three explanations (19:2-21:4) are a sermon on renewal: as an old man who inherits a fortune gets up and stands (20:2), so believers renewed by the revelation grow young.

a: you have not thrown your worries on the Lord
p: Lake's margin gives Psalm 55:22 and 1 Peter 5:7.
b: 'Throw every worry you have onto him, because you matter to him' (1 Peter 5:7); 'Throw your load on the LORD, and he will provide for you' (Psalm 55:22). Hermas's Greek epiriptein ... tas merimnas epi ton kyrion is close to 1 Peter and to the Greek Psalm (54:23 in Swete: epiripson epi kyrion tēn merimnan sou). The same words return in 23:4-5, where Hermas does what is asked here and escapes the beast.

a: listlessness
p: Greek akēdia, 'not caring', a weary indifference.
b: Akēdia (plural here) is a weary indifference, 'not caring'. Hermas already describes it: believers 'weakened by the business of everyday life' who have 'given themselves over' to it and 'grown old' with their griefs.

a: the figure of the first vision
p: Greek typos, 'type, pattern', is the site's word 'figure'.
b: Typos is the mark left by a blow, then a pattern or a sign of something else. The site renders it 'figure', as in Romans 5:14 ('Adam is a figure of the one who was coming'). Hermas uses it for the meaning of a vision (here and 22:1; 23:5; 24:6: the beast is 'a figure of the great suffering').

a: the world too is held together by four elements
p: The couch's four legs recall the four elements, which Hermas takes as common knowledge.
b: Hermas takes it as common knowledge that the world is held together by four elements (stoicheia; Lake: 'the world is controlled by four elements'); he does not name them. He uses the idea in passing, to say that the couch, like the world, stands firm on four supports. The Wisdom of Solomon's sage knows 'how the elements work' (Wisdom of Solomon 7:17), and 2 Peter says 'the elements will burn and be dissolved' at the end (2 Peter 3:10).

a: the Campanian Way
p: A road out of Rome; the place was about ten stades off the main road.
b: Lake: 'I was going into the country by the Via Campana.' The Greek hē hodos hē kampanē is 'the Campanian road', a road out of Rome. The place was 'about ten stades' (gloss: a little over a mile) from the public highway and easy to reach. Hermas gives real-sounding directions: the vision of the beast happens on an ordinary walk into the country.

a: something like the echo of a voice
p: An answer comes 'like the echo of a voice': a voice heard, with no speaker seen.
b: Lake: 'an answer came to me as an echo of my voice'. The voice is heard but no speaker is seen, as when a voice answers Jesus from heaven and some hear only thunder (John 12:28-29). The word is short and sharp: 'Do not be double-minded, Hermas' (repeated in 22:7). It prepares him to face the beast.

a: a huge beast like some sea monster
t: The beast like a sea monster
p: A beast 'like a kētos' with fiery locusts: Lake calls it 'some Leviathan'.
b: Kētos is a sea monster, the word for Jonah's great fish (Matthew 12:40) and in the Greek Bible for monsters of the deep. Lake translates 'like some Leviathan', the chaos beast of Job 41 and Isaiah 27:1. Fiery locusts come from its mouth, like the locusts from the smoke in Revelation 9:3. Revelation's beast comes 'up out of the sea' (Revelation 13:1), and Daniel's four beasts climb out of the sea (Daniel 7:3). Hermas's beast is explained in 23:5: 'a figure of the great suffering that is coming'.
r: Revelation 13:1-2; Daniel 7:3; Revelation 9:3; Job 41:1; Isaiah 27:1; Joel 2:1-11

a: its head looked like a piece of pottery
p: Greek keramos is 'clay, a pot, a tile'; Lake: 'its head was like a piece of pottery'.
b: The sense is uncertain. Keramos can mean potter's clay, an earthen jar or a roof tile. It may describe the shape of the head (round like a jar), its color, or fragile, breakable stuff, which would fit a beast that cannot harm the faithful. The beast is 'about a hundred feet long' (Greek numeral ρ, 100).

a: I put on the faith of the Lord
p: Hermas faces the beast 'clothed' in faith, like the believer's armor in Paul.
b: Paul tells believers to 'wear the breastplate of faith and love' (1 Thessalonians 5:8) and to take up 'the shield of faith' (Ephesians 6:16). Hermas 'put on' faith and 'gave himself up' to face a beast whose rush could 'wreck a city'. Faith is the first of the seven women (16:3).

a: dressed as if she were coming out of a bridal room
p: Lake's margin gives Psalm 19:5 and Revelation 21:2; the Church now appears as a bride.
b: The site's Psalm 19:5 has the sun coming out 'like a bridegroom from the wedding room', and Revelation sees the new Jerusalem 'made ready like a bride dressed in her finery for her husband' (Revelation 21:2). Hermas's young woman is dressed all in white, veiled to the forehead, with a turban (mitra) for a head covering. But 'her hair was white': the old age of the first vision is not wholly gone (compare 18:5).

a: whose name is Thegri
t: Thegri, the angel over the beasts
p: An angel otherwise unknown; Lake reports a proposal that the name comes from the Hebrew for 'shut'.
b: Lake's footnote: 'No other mention of this Angel is found in Jewish or Christian literature, and no suitable meaning has been suggested for Thegri. Dr. Rendel Harris suggests Segri as an emendation, connecting it with the Hebrew word meaning "to shut" (sagar), found in Dan. 6, 22.' Daniel 6 is in Aramaic, and its verb there (Daniel 6:22, 6:23 in the Aramaic numbering) is segar, the same root as the Hebrew. The angel 'shut its mouth', as Daniel says, 'My God sent his angel to shut the lions' mouths' (Daniel 6:22). Jewish writings gave angels charge over parts of nature (1 Enoch 20); this one rules the beasts.

a: you can be saved through nothing but the great and glorious Name
p: Lake's margin gives Acts 4:12: no other name in which we must be saved.
b: 'Nowhere under heaven is there another name given among human beings, a name in which we must be saved' (Acts 4:12). Hermas trusts the 'great and glorious Name' (see 9:9), and the Church says that is why he escaped. The first hand of Sinaiticus reads differently here (see the variant on 'great').

a: It would have been better for them not to be born
p: Lake's margin gives Jesus' word about his betrayer, Matthew 26:24.
b: Jesus says of the man who hands him over: 'Better for that man never to have been born' (Matthew 26:24; Mark 14:21). Hermas uses it of those who hear these words 'and refuse to listen' (Greek parakousasin). God 'sends whips' on the double-minded: punishment that is meant to correct (compare 7:1, 'trained with a training that is right').

a: The black is this world you live in
p: Black, fire-and-blood, gold and white: this world, its destruction, the faithful tested, the age to come.
b: The colors on the beast's head (22:10) tell the story of the end in order. Black is the present world; fire and blood its coming destruction (24:3; compare 'blood and fire and pillars of smoke', Joel 2:30); gold the believers tested in it; white the age to come. Revelation's four horsemen also ride in four colors (white, red, black and pale, Revelation 6:1-8), though with other meanings, and Zechariah's horses and chariots are colored (Zechariah 1:8; 6:2-3).

a: this world must be destroyed by blood and fire
p: The world's end by fire, as in 2 Peter 3:7 and 3:10.
b: 'The heavens and the earth of now ... have been put in storage for fire' (2 Peter 3:7), and 'the elements will burn and be dissolved' (2 Peter 3:10). Joel's signs of the day of the LORD are 'blood and fire' (Joel 2:30), quoted by Peter at Pentecost (Acts 2:19).

a: just as gold is tested by fire
p: Lake's margin gives 1 Peter 1:7 and compares Sirach 2:5, Proverbs 17:3 and Job 23:10.
b: Peter: faith's 'proving is worth far more than gold, which perishes even though fire tests it' (1 Peter 1:7). Sirach: 'Fire is where gold is proved' (Sirach 2:5). 'Gold in the furnace' (Proverbs 17:3). Lake's footnote on 'you who live in the midst of them': 'The "them" means "fire and blood"; but the construction of the sentence is awkward.' So the Plain English Translation names the blood and the fire of 24:3, and 'by them' is the agent: the believers are put through the fire by the blood and the fire themselves. Lake's margin beside these verses also gives 2 Peter 2:20, where people 'have escaped the filth of the world by knowing the Lord'; here the gold part is 'you who have escaped this world'. Those who go through the fire throw off grief and distress as gold throws off dross, and become 'useful for the building of the tower': the gold layer is the church now.
r: 1 Peter 1:7; 1 Peter 4:12; Sirach 2:5; Proverbs 17:3; Job 23:10; Malachi 3:2-3; 2 Peter 2:20

a: But if you are willing, it will be nothing
p: The coming suffering can be 'nothing' if the believers are willing: is it avoided, or only made harmless?
b: Two readings are possible. The persecution may not happen at all if the church repents, as Nineveh's repentance turned away judgment (Jonah 3:10). Or it will come but do no harm, as the beast lay down and let Hermas pass (22:9), and as 23:5 says they will 'escape it' if they repent with all their heart. The Church's last words, 'Remember what was written before', point back to the little book of Vision 2 (6:2-7:4).

a: Then suddenly an inheritance is left to him
p: A parable of renewal: an old man who has given up hope is made young again by an unexpected inheritance.
b: The young man calls this a parabolē, 'parable' (20:1). The old man had given up because of weakness and poverty; news of an inheritance gets him up, 'puts on strength', and makes his worn-out spirit new. So the revelation is the believers' inheritance: they have been renewed 'because he had compassion on you' (20:3). The picture is close to Psalm 103:5 ('like the eagle, you grow young again') and Isaiah 40:31, and to the 'inheritance that cannot decay' of 1 Peter 1:4. Hermas's readers, worn down by business and grief (19:3), are told that God's gift can make even the old stand up.
